cards: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who seized power after the French Revolution and ruled as Emperor of the French.
Simón Bolívar was a Venezuelan leader of the wars of independence against Spain, known as the Liberator.
Napoleon III, nephew of Napoleon Bonaparte, was President of France and then Emperor of the French during the Second Empire from 1852 to 1870.
Karl Marx was a German philosopher, political theorist and revolutionary socialist whose theory of historical materialism analysed social change through class struggle and predicted that communism…
Victoria was queen of the United Kingdom from 1837 to 1901 and empress of India from 1876.
James Madison was the fourth president of the United States, from 1809 to 1817, and a principal author of the US Constitution and the Bill of Rights.
Otto von Bismarck was a Prussian statesman who unified Germany and served as the first chancellor of the German Empire.
Cecil Rhodes was a British businessman and politician in southern Africa who made a fortune in Kimberley diamonds through De Beers and in gold.
Friedrich Engels was a German philosopher, social and political theorist and revolutionary socialist, born in Barmen, Prussia, to a prosperous mercantile family.
Giuseppe Garibaldi was an Italian revolutionary and soldier, born in Nice.
Menelik II was Emperor of Ethiopia from 1889 to 1913.
José de San Martín was an Argentine general who led the liberation of southern South America from Spain.
Ranjit Singh was the founder and Maharaja of the Sikh Empire, who lived from 1780 to 1839.
Agustín de Iturbide was a Mexican royalist officer who changed sides in 1821 and, with the insurgent Vicente Guerrero, issued the Plan of Iguala, which brought Mexico independence from Spain.
Antonio José de Sucre was a Venezuelan general and Simón Bolívar's closest lieutenant in the Spanish American wars of independence.
John Stuart Mill was an English philosopher, economist and Liberal member of Parliament, the most influential British liberal thinker of the nineteenth century.
Rafael Carrera was a Guatemalan caudillo of humble origins who in 1837 led a peasant revolt against the liberal government of the Federal Republic of Central America.
Francisco Morazán was a Honduran general and Liberal leader who captured Guatemala City in 1829 and was president of the Federal Republic of Central America from 1830 to 1839.
Alexander I of Russia was emperor of the Russian Empire from 1801 to 1825.
Alexis de Tocqueville was a French political thinker, historian and politician.
Ernest Renan was a French scholar of Semitic languages, historian of religion and essayist.
Thomas Stamford Raffles was a British official of the East India Company.
Lord Dalhousie was Governor-General of India from 1848 to 1856.
Muhammad Ali of Egypt was an Albanian officer of the Ottoman army who became governor of Egypt in 1805 and founded a dynasty that ruled until 1952.
Richard Wagner was a German composer and theatre director whose operas, which he called music dramas, transformed European music.
Tewodros II was Emperor of Ethiopia from 1855 until his death in 1868.
Abraham Lincoln was the 16th president of the United States, from 1861 until his assassination in 1865.
Andrew Jackson was an American general and the seventh President of the United States, serving from 1829 to 1837.
Andries Pretorius was a Voortrekker leader who commanded the Boer force that defeated the Zulu army of Dingane at Blood River in December 1838, securing the Natalia Republic.
Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, was the leading statesman of the Kingdom of Sardinia and the first prime minister of united Italy.
David Livingstone was a Scottish missionary and explorer of central and southern Africa.
Franz Joseph I was Emperor of Austria and King of Hungary (r. 1848–1916).
Henry Morton Stanley was a Welsh-American journalist and explorer who found David Livingstone in 1871 and crossed Africa in 1874–1877, following the Lualaba and Congo to the Atlantic with help from…
Samori Ture was a West African Muslim leader who built a large state, often called the Wassoulou Empire, in the late nineteenth century.
Theodore Roosevelt was the 26th president of the United States, from 1901 to 1909.
Alexander Pushkin was a Russian poet, playwright and novelist of the early nineteenth century, widely regarded as the founder of modern Russian literature.
Dadabhai Naoroji was an Indian political leader, economist and scholar from a Parsi family of Bombay.
Jean-Pierre Boyer was president of Haiti from 1818 to 1843.
Prince Klemens von Metternich was Austrian foreign minister from 1809 and chancellor from 1821 until 1848.
Leopold von Ranke was a German historian and a founder of modern source-based history.
